subject: Covariate modeling with rare species - Camera Trap

messages.author: 168f21f5ce6ef78a
messages.subject: Covariate modeling with rare species - Camera Trap
parts:
Hi all,

I am currently doing the analysis from our camera trap survey dataset done in 2020-2021 in one protected area, using the CTDS methodology. Here is the list of number of independent events we got for each species:
- Variable squirrel: 250
- Berdmore's squirrel: 152
- Chevrotain: 89
- Siamese fireback: 83
- Wild pig: 65
- Common palm civet: 60
- Northern threeshrew: 54
- Red junglefowl: 48
- Long-tailed macaque: 48
- White-crested laughingthrush: 30
- Leopard cat: 27
- Malayan porcupine: 18
- Northern Red Muntjac: 15

As you can see, I will be able to produce population estimates for the 4 first species, but the other species don't have enough independent records to produce population estimates. I saw this alternative form of analysis where the species is treated as a covariate in the modelling of the detection function, for the line transect survey Buckland conducted (https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-spec-covar/species-covariate-distill.html). I was wondering if this form of analysis would also be applicable for my camera trap dataset, to be able to get population estimates for species with not enough records. 

Thank you for your help,

Emeline Auda

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: {Suspected Spam} [distance-sampling] Covariate modeling with rare species - Camera Trap
parts:
Emeline

In principle, your suggestion could work for CTDS analysis. Species that are combined into the covariate analysis you suggest would need to share a common key function (half normal or hazard rate).  I've not attempted such an analysis with CTDS data.

Recognise much of the uncertainty in CTDS analyses stems from encounter rate variability, rather than difficulties with detection function modelling.  You don't mention the number of camera stations used in this survey; I might have concerns about the estimation of encounter rate variance, but that is largely a function of the survey design.
